Home/Revision rhinoplasty

Revision rhinoplasty

Revision rhinoplasty is surgery on a nose that has been operated on before, to correct a problem with its shape, its breathing, or both. It is usually more demanding than a first operation, because the natural structure has changed and less cartilage may be available.

At a glance

Operating time
About 3 to 5 hours
Anaesthesia
General
Hospital stay
Same day or one night
Timing
Usually at least 12 months after the previous surgery
Book a consultation

Common reasons for revision

  • blockage or breathing difficulty that started or worsened after previous surgery
  • over-reduction of the bridge or a collapsed area
  • an asymmetric, over-rotated or drooping tip
  • remaining deviation or visible asymmetry

Why we wait

The nose needs time for swelling to resolve and tissues to settle, typically at least 12 months. Waiting allows an accurate assessment of the real result and leaves the tissues better prepared for further surgery. Severe breathing problems may justify earlier intervention, depending on assessment.

Cartilage grafts

Revision often needs cartilage to rebuild support. The first source is septal cartilage if any remains; otherwise it may be taken from the ear or a rib. This is decided at consultation after examination.

Realistic expectations

The aim of revision surgery is a clear improvement in form and function, not perfection. Results depend on skin quality, scar tissue and the remaining structure, and recovery is usually somewhat longer than after a first rhinoplasty.

Frequently asked questions

How long should I wait after my first surgery?

Usually at least 12 months, so swelling settles and the true result is clear. This may differ if there is a severe breathing problem.

Can breathing and shape be corrected together?

Yes, and that is common. The septum and nasal valves are addressed within the same plan.

Will I need rib cartilage?

Not always. It depends on how much septal cartilage remains and how much support is needed, and is decided after examination.

Should I bring my previous operative report?

Yes, if possible. The report and pre-operative photos help a great deal in understanding what changed and planning the repair.
